sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll have a documented, personal AI workflow playbook that covers which tool you use for what, your daily automation routine, and the specific automations you plan to build next.

## Reviewing What You've Built

In Part 10 you covered five different automation layers:

**n8n** — Free, powerful, open-source. Native AI nodes. Best for: complex multi-step workflows, AI processing, batch jobs, anything where you want full control at no cost.

**Zapier** — Most polished, easiest setup, 6,000+ integrations. Best for: quick connections between mainstream apps, non-technical users, one-step automations. AI step requires paid plan.

**Make** — Visual canvas, generous free tier. Best for: teams that think visually, complex data transformations, calling any API via the HTTP module.

**AI-Assisted Git** — Using Claude to write commit messages, PR descriptions, changelogs. Best for: developers who want better git history with zero extra effort.

**GitHub Actions** — Code-based CI/CD. Best for: automated testing, deployment, and AI review on every push. Requires a GitHub repo.

## Decision Framework: Which Tool for Which Job?

Use this as a starting point — adjust based on what you've found works for you:

| Situation | Best tool |
|-----------|----------|
| Connecting two cloud apps, no AI needed | Zapier free tier or n8n |
| AI processing step in a workflow, cost matters | n8n (free AI nodes) |
| AI processing step, fastest setup matters | Zapier (paid) |
| Calling a REST API with no native module | Make HTTP module or n8n HTTP node |
| Recurring scheduled jobs with AI | n8n Cloud |
| Git commit messages and PRs | Claude Code in terminal |
| Automated testing and deployment | GitHub Actions |
| Code review on every PR | GitHub Actions + AI review action |

The honest answer is: most people pick **one** of n8n, Zapier, or Make and use it for 90% of their automation needs. The git and GitHub Actions patterns apply to everyone writing code regardless of which automation platform they use.

**The single best automation you can build:** A daily morning digest. Pick the information sources you check manually every morning (email, news, GitHub notifications, calendar). Wire them through an AI summarization step. Deliver to your inbox by 7am. You've just saved 15-20 minutes per day — over a year that's 90+ hours returned to your life.

## The Personal AI Stack

Your "personal AI stack" is your specific combination of tools that handles your work. It's personal — someone who manages client projects needs different automations than a developer shipping code or a student managing research.

The questions to ask:
1. **What do I do repeatedly?** (from your audit in lesson 10-1)
2. **Which of those could be fully automated?** (no human judgment needed)
3. **Which could be semi-automated?** (AI does the first draft, I review)
4. **For the ones I want to automate — which tool fits?**
5. **What's the one automation that would save me the most time?** (Start there.)

Don't try to automate everything at once. Build one thing, let it run for a week, verify it's doing what you want, then build the next one.

sections.title: Design Your Personal AI Workflow
sections.content:
Create `notes/my-ai-workflow.md` in your VS Code project. Write your personal AI workflow playbook using this structure:

```markdown
# My AI Workflow

## Tools I Use
- Automation platform: [n8n / Zapier / Make — and why]
- Git workflow: [which AI git patterns I've adopted]
- CI/CD: [GitHub Actions — yes/no, what workflows are active]

## Daily Routine
- Morning: [which automation runs, what it delivers]
- Before starting work: [any AI-assisted checks or briefs]
- During development: [git patterns, Claude Code use]
- End of day: [any wrap-up automations]

## Active Automations
[List each running workflow: what it does, when it runs, what tool it's on]

## Next 3 Automations I'll Build
1. [Automation]: [Tool]: [Why this one next]
2. [Automation]: [Tool]: [Why]
3. [Automation]: [Tool]: [Why]

## Tool Routing
- Research questions → [tool]
- Writing help → [tool]
- Code work → [tool]
- Email management → [tool]
- Automation → [tool]
- [add your own rows]

## What I Don't Automate (and why)
[Be honest — some things should stay manual]
```

This document is the most practical output of Part 10. It turns what you've learned into a living system you'll actually use. Update it whenever you add a new automation or change a tool.

sections.title: Workshop A — Personal Workflow Inventory
sections.content:
Map your complete personal AI-assisted workflow.

**Step 1 — List every AI tool** you use regularly in your work:
- In-editor assistance (Copilot, Continue.dev, Tabnine)
- Terminal/CLI (Claude Code)
- Chat (Claude.ai, ChatGPT)
- Automation (n8n, Zapier, Make)
- Specialty tools (Cursor, Windsurf, etc.)

**Step 2 — For each tool**, estimate:
- Hours per week saved
- Most frequent use cases
- Biggest friction points

**Step 3 — Draw your workflow diagram:** For a typical work day, when do you reach for which tool? Where are the handoffs?

**Step 4 — Ask Claude:** *"Based on this AI tool stack [describe it], what important gaps exist? What workflows are inefficient because I'm using the wrong tool or switching between too many tools?"*

**Step 5 — Identify your single biggest workflow inefficiency** to address this week.

sections.title: Workshop B — Design Your Ideal AI Workflow
sections.content:
Design the AI-assisted workflow you want, then identify the gaps to close.

**Step 1 — Choose a major type of work** you do regularly: software development, content creation, research, client work.

**Step 2 — Design your IDEAL workflow** for this work type:
- What AI tools are involved at each stage?
- Where does AI assist vs where does it automate?
- What human decisions remain?
- What does the output look like?

**Step 3 — Compare to your CURRENT workflow:** What's different between ideal and current?

**Step 4 — Identify the 3 changes** that would most close the gap between ideal and current.

**Step 5 — For the highest-priority change**, ask Claude Code to help implement it:
"I want to add [specific improvement] to my workflow. Design the implementation: what tools, configuration, or automation would I build?"

sections.title: Workshop C — Workflow Anti-Patterns
sections.content:
Identify and eliminate common AI workflow anti-patterns.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** *"What are the most common anti-patterns in AI-assisted workflows — things people do that reduce productivity or quality? For each, describe: the pattern, why people fall into it, and the better alternative."*

**Step 2 — Check yourself:** Which of these anti-patterns do YOU currently practice?

**Step 3 — Common anti-patterns to specifically check:**
- Copy-pasting AI output without review
- Using chat AI for tasks that need agentic tools
- Asking AI to do 5 things in one prompt instead of iterating
- Not giving AI enough context on the first try
- Switching tools mid-task instead of staying in one tool

**Step 4 — For each anti-pattern you identified in yourself**, define the specific behaviour change you'll make.

**Step 5 — Schedule a 30-day review** to check if you've actually changed those behaviours.

sections.title: Workshop D — Document and Share Your Workflow
sections.content:
Create a workflow document that could help a colleague adopt AI tools effectively.

**Step 1 — Write a workflow guide** for your primary work type:
```markdown
# My AI-Assisted [Work Type] Workflow

## Overview
[2-3 sentence summary of your workflow]

## Tools Used
[List tools and their roles]

## Daily Workflow
### Morning
- [Step 1: which tool, what for]
- [Step 2: ...]

### During work
- [How AI assists the main work]

### Review/output
- [How you review AI-generated content]
```

**Step 2 — Ask Claude to review the guide:** *"Review this workflow guide. What would confuse someone new to AI tools? What important context is missing?"*

**Step 3 — Refine the guide** based on feedback.

**Step 4 — Share with one colleague** this week. What is their reaction? What questions do they have?

**Step 5 — Update the guide** based on their feedback.

sections.question: You have 6 different AI tools in your workflow. Switching between them takes 2-3 minutes each time and breaks concentration. What is the most effective solution?
options: Buy a faster computer to reduce switching time
Designate primary tool(s) for each task type and only switch when the primary tool truly cannot do the job — reduce tool sprawl
Use only one AI tool for everything
Accept that tool switching is inevitable in a complex workflow
sections.explanation: Context switching is a real productivity cost — not just the mechanical time but the cognitive reset required. The solution isn't to use one tool for everything (different tools genuinely excel at different tasks) but to be deliberate about when you switch. Define: "I use tool X for Y tasks, tool Z for W tasks" and resist the temptation to switch "just to try" in the middle of a task. Reduce your active tool set to 2-3 that cover 90% of your needs.

sections.question: You've spent Part 10 learning workflow automation. What is the most important mindset for maintaining these automations long-term?
options: Build as many automations as possible to maximise time savings
Treat automations like code: they need maintenance, testing, and occasional review — they will break as APIs change, and a broken automation can be worse than doing the task manually
Avoid complex automations — simple ones are more reliable
Automate everything and review failures quarterly
sections.explanation: Automations are maintenance commitments, not one-time builds. APIs change, services update, data formats evolve — an automation built last year may silently produce wrong results today. Budget time for automation maintenance: monthly checks that outputs are still correct, quarterly reviews of whether the automation still matches the actual process, and immediate investigation when an automation's output changes unexpectedly. A well-maintained automation saves time; an unmaintained one creates hidden errors.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 10-7.** You've documented your personal AI workflow and automation strategy. Next: lesson 10-8 puts everything together in a real project — building, deploying, and auto-updating a live website. **Skill tip:** The workflows you designed in this lesson are perfect candidates for Claude Code custom skills — save them as skill files in `~/.claude/commands/` and trigger them with a single command instead of re-building the context each time. Part 20 teaches exactly how to do this, including skills that chain workflows together.
